title: Memories can persist through complete brain regeneration in planaria

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Memories can persist through complete brain regeneration in planaria

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In some organisms such as planaria, memories (prior knowledge and behavioural tendencies) can apparently persist after the complete regeneration of the brain, being transferred onto the newly constructed brain.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Levin M 2022, Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds › Cognition: Changing the Subject

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Not only that, but memories can apparently persist following the complete regeneration of brains in some organisms (McConnell et al., 1959; Corning, 1966; Shomrat and Levin, 2013) such as planaria, in which prior knowledge and behavioral tendencies are somehow transferred onto a newly-constructed brain.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Levin M, “Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds”, Frontiers in systems neuroscience (2022), doi:10.3389/fnsys.2022.768201; section “Cognition: Changing the Subject”. Scope: Planarian flatworms trained before decapitation and head regeneration

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2022-tame-02: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Behavioral retention after brain regeneration is operationalizable, and several published studies provide relevant measurements. Their small samples, methodological heterogeneity, and alternative explanations make the general claim only partly resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare pre- and post-regeneration performance of trained and untrained planaria on the same behavioral assay, controlling for retraining, handling, innate bias, and regenerated sensory capacity.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Raw trial-level data are sparse.

Post-regeneration performance can reflect bias or rapid relearning rather than transferred memory.

Historical studies use heterogeneous and sometimes disputed training assays.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.62
data adequacy: 0.4
operationalizability: 0.9
data existence: 0.55
analysis feasibility: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Memory here has a workable behavioral meaning: faster return to criterion after training, measured again after the head regenerates. Published tables from the automated familiarization study and older training papers contain summary counts, scattered across journals rather than in one archive. Those summaries can be re-read for effect direction, and they leave the main confounds and the raw latencies unchecked.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare time-to-criterion or savings after regeneration between animals trained before decapitation and naive regenerates; persistence holds if trained animals relearn faster after a new brain is built, with motility equated.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Classical manual studies and the 2013 familiarization assay do not cover the same tasks.

Residual body tissue, sensitization, and one-tailed tests can mimic savings without a memory stored outside the original brain.

Raw tracking logs from the automated assay were not deposited.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.5
analysis feasibility: 0.45
discriminating power: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.4
